section: F-LIC: FPGA-based Learned Image Compression with a Fine-grained Pipeline
text: Heming Sun 1,2,3 , Qingyang Yi 4 , Fangzheng Lin 1 , Lu Yu 2 , Jiro Katto 1 , and Masahiro Fujita 4,5 1 Waseda University, Tokyo, Japan; 2 Zhejiang University, Zhejiang, China; 3 JST, PRESTO, Saitama, Japan; 4 The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan; 5 AIST, Tokyo, Japan Recently, learned image compression (LIC) has shown a superior ability in the compression ratio as well as the quality of the reconstructed image. By adopting the framework of variational autoencoder, LIC [1] can outperform the intra prediction of the latest traditional coding standard VVC. To accelerate the coding speed, most LIC frameworks are operated on GPU with the floating-point arithmetic. However, the mismatch of floating-point calculation results on various hardware platforms will cause the decoding error if encoding and decoding are performed on different platforms. Therefore, LIC with a fixed-point arithmetic [2][3] is highly required. This paper gives an FPGA design for a LIC with 8-bit fixed-point quantization. Different from existing FPGA accelerators [4][5][6], we propose a fine-grained pipeline architecture to realize high DSP efficiency. Cascading DSP and the deconvolution with zero skipping are also developed to enhance the hardware performance. Fig. 1 depicts the neural network structure of encoding and decoding. We use the hyper-prior structure in [3]. The encoding is composed of analysis transform (AT), hyper analysis transform (HA) and hyper synthesis transform (HS). AT transforms the original image x to latent code y. HA transforms the latent y to latent z which is transferred to the host PC for the range encoding. HS generates mean μ and scale σ of y, and send them to the host PC. The decoding is composed of synthesis transform (ST) and HS. At first, a range decoder is used to recover z based on the bitstream. z is then input to the HS to generate the μ and σ of y. Another range decoder is used to recover y. Finally, y is input to ST to produce the reconstructed image x'. Fig. 2 shows the overall architecture and a pipeline example. All the parameters are stored once in the external memory, and input image is transferred to DDR during the execution. Input buffer stores the demanded rows for the first layer, and output buffer stores the computation results of the final layer. To support the pipelining, each layer possesses its own processing elements which are mainly composed of multiply accumulate unit DSP. We exploit parallelism from three dimensions: kernel width (k), input channel (c), and output channel (m). After traversing all the input channels, output channels and kernel height, one output element can be produced. Therefore, required cycles for producing one row is a function of c, m and k. A sophisticated selection of c and m will lead to the high DSP efficiency. An adaptive activation (act) buffer between two consecutive layers is designed to support a fine granularity for DSP allocation. The act buffer is composed of several row buffers, and the ping-pong mechanism is utilized to rotate the writing and reading for each row buffer. To support the flexible selection of channel parallelism, we use the crossbar for the input and output side of row buffer. Multiple BRAM (RAMB18K) slices are built to store the results of all the channels. Each BRAM can be configured as 8b×2048, 16b×1024 or 32b×512. To increase the BRAM efficiency in the depth-wise, we start to configure the BRAM from the shallowest shape 32b×512. In the case that there is an address conflict for writing or reading, we halve the width and double the depth. First four layers in AT are used to explain the pipeline scheduling. For each layer, the computation will start after required output is produced from the previous layer. A maximum cycle budget (T/2T/4T in Fig. 2) is set for each layer to align the row processing. The budget is inversely proportional to the output height. DSP efficiency for each layer can be calculated as the ratio of actual working cycles to the maximum cycle budget. Fig. 3 depicts the structure of processing elements. c input channels and m output channels are processed in parallel. For a specific input channel and output channel, the MAC operation for the kernel width is computed in parallel. Following the weight stationary mechanism, each input activation (iact) is multiplied with all the kernels in the width-wise. Two weights from two output channels share one DSP to multiply with the same iact. In addition, we propose the cascading DSP (casDSP) to calculate the kernel-width-wise partial sum (psum) inside DSP. The instruction of DSP is configured as (A+D)xB+C. Two weights are allocated in the LSB of A-port and MSB of D-port respectively to avoid the occlusion as much as possible. B-port is used for the iact, and C-port is used to transfer two psum results. When using DSP48E1 which supports 25x18b, the margin for the lower psum is only 17b. In the case of kernel width being larger than two, there will be an overflow problem. To avoid the overflow, before transferring the lower psum to the next cascading, the MSB is split so that the significant digits are within 16b. An extra chain is used to add the split MSB. Finally, the summed MSB is merged with lower psum. For the higher psum, there is no need to split MSB since the bitwidth of C-port can be as large as 48b. Fig. 4 presents the deconvolution manipulation with stride being two and kernel being 5x5. Given that the input is 3x3, in the case of stride being two, it is first dilated to double size by inserting zero elements. The dilated input is then convolved with the kernel to produce the results. We propose two methods to skip the calculation with inserted zero inputs. 1) Regarding the column-wise, each convolution contains three or two non-zero input columns alternately along with the striding window, thus we provide one casDSP with three DSPs and one casDSP with two DSPs individually. By broadcasting each iact to both casDSP, the results of two neighboring columns can be generated simultaneously. 2) In our dataflow, the kernel is traversed row by row. During the traverse, for each specific row of the kernel, it will only be used in one of two convolutions of adjacent rows. Between the two convolutions, the convolution results with two nonzero input rows are produced at first, followed by the results requiring three non-zero input rows. Fig. 5 evaluates the DSP efficiency. Due to the flexibility of the input and output channel parallelism, we can achieve higher DSP efficiency compared with the prior pipeline work [6] which restricts the channel parallelism as power of two. In the case of 720p@41fps encoding and 720p@36fps decoding on VCU118, DSP efficiency surpasses 90% for almost all the layers. For other evaluation boards, various coding speed can be achieved according to the resource scale of the board. However, DSP efficiency is larger than 90% on average for all the encoding and decoding cases. Fig. 6 shows the comparison with other LIC implementations.

section: F-LIC: FPGA-based Learned Image Compression with a Fine-grained Pipeline
text: Compared with [7], our method owns better PSNR with lower bit per pixel (bpp). Moreover, we can achieve 1.31x-1.49x faster frame per second (fps) for encoding, and 4.95x-5.61x faster fps for decoding. Much faster decoding is due to the proposed zero skipping in the deconvolution and a relatively light LIC model. Our design also consumes lower power per frame than [7]. We also compare with an embedded GPU (Jetson Xavier NX) and a powerful GPU (RTX 3090). Though floating precision achieves a little bit better coding gain, it hinders the cross-platform coding possibility. Compared with Jetson, 4.43x-5.81x higher fps can be achieved. With a former process technology used in the FPGA chips, we still reaches comparable power efficiency with Jetson. Compared with RTX 3090, we obtain up to 2.15x faster speed. Power efficiency is also better simply because the utilization of GPU is low. We also provide resource utilization. The operating frequency is 200MHz in all the cases.
